subject: Cardiovascular
subtopic: Aortic dissection and traumatic aortic rupture
vignette: A 26-year-old unrestrained man is brought to the emergency department after a high-speed motor vehicle collision in which his car struck a bridge abutment. He is hypotensive, his femoral pulses are weak compared with his radial pulses, and chest x-ray shows a widened mediastinum.
question: At which site is his aortic injury most likely located?

options.text: The aortic root, just above the sinuses of Valsalva
The origin of the brachiocephalic artery
The abdominal aorta, distal to the renal arteries
The proximal abdominal aorta at the diaphragmatic hiatus
The aortic isthmus, just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery

explanation_correct: Traumatic aortic rupture results from trauma and/or deceleration injury, such as a motor vehicle accident or significant fall. It occurs most commonly at the aortic isthmus — the proximal descending aorta just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery — where the relatively mobile aortic arch is suddenly decelerated against the fixed descending aorta. A widened mediastinum on x-ray is the classic clue.

explanation_incorrect.A: The aortic root is affected in Stanford type A dissection and syphilitic aneurysm, not in deceleration injury, which favors the isthmus.
explanation_incorrect.B: Injury at the brachiocephalic origin is not the typical site of deceleration injury; the isthmus just distal to the left subclavian is.
explanation_incorrect.C: The infrarenal abdominal aorta is the typical site of abdominal aortic aneurysm, not traumatic rupture from deceleration.
explanation_incorrect.D: The diaphragmatic hiatus is not the classic deceleration injury site; the mobile arch shears against the descending aorta at the isthmus.

educationalObjective: Localize traumatic aortic rupture to the aortic isthmus, just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery, after deceleration injury.

subject: Cardiovascular
subtopic: Aortic dissection and traumatic aortic rupture
vignette: A 63-year-old man with long-standing hypertension presents with sudden-onset tearing chest pain radiating to his back. CT angiography shows a longitudinal intimal tear with a false lumen confined to the descending aorta, beginning just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery. His blood pressure is 186/104 mm Hg and he is neurologically intact.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Observation with serial imaging and no medications

explanation_correct: This is a Stanford type B (distal) dissection: it involves only the descending aorta, below the left subclavian artery. The treatment of type B dissection is β-blockers to reduce the force of left ventricular contraction and shear stress, then vasodilators to further control blood pressure. In contrast, Stanford type A dissections involving the ascending aorta are treated surgically.

explanation_incorrect.B: Immediate surgery is the treatment of Stanford type A (ascending) dissection; type B dissections limited to the descending aorta are managed medically.
explanation_incorrect.C: Thrombolysis is used for ischemic stroke and myocardial infarction, not dissection, and could precipitate fatal aortic rupture.
explanation_incorrect.D: Balloon valvuloplasty treats stenotic valves; it has no role in repairing an aortic intimal tear.
explanation_incorrect.E: Untreated severe hypertension will propagate the false lumen; medical therapy with β-blockade is required even for type B dissections.

educationalObjective: Treat Stanford type B dissection (descending aorta only, below the left subclavian) with β-blockers then vasodilators.

subject: Cardiovascular
subtopic: Aortic dissection and traumatic aortic rupture
vignette: A 57-year-old woman with Marfan syndrome presents with sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back. Examination reveals a new high-pitched early diastolic murmur at the right sternal border with a wide pulse pressure (158/54 mm Hg), muffled heart sounds, and distended neck veins with a hypotensive blood pressure when inhaling. CT angiography shows a dissection flap involving the ascending aorta.
question: Which of the following best describes the management of and a potential complication of this patient's condition?

options.text: β-blockers then vasodilators; complications are limited to renal artery ischemia
Systemic thrombolysis; the main complication is embolic stroke
Observation with serial imaging; the main complication is chronic stable angina
Surgical repair; potential complications include acute aortic regurgitation and cardiac tamponade
Antibiotic therapy; the main complication is septic embolization

explanation_correct: This is a Stanford type A (proximal) dissection, involving the ascending aorta. Stanford type A dissections are treated with surgery because they may extend to the aortic arch or descending aorta and may result in acute aortic regurgitation (from dilation of the aortic root and annulus, explaining her diastolic murmur and wide pulse pressure) or cardiac tamponade (hemopericardium, explaining muffled heart sounds, distended neck veins, and inspiratory fall in blood pressure).

explanation_incorrect.A: β-blockers then vasodilators is the treatment of Stanford type B dissections, which involve only the descending aorta; an ascending dissection requires surgery, and its feared complications are acute aortic regurgitation and tamponade, not just renal ischemia.
explanation_incorrect.B: Thrombolysis has no role in dissection and could worsen bleeding into the wall or pericardium; embolic stroke is a possible complication but does not define management.
explanation_incorrect.C: Observation alone is inappropriate for an ascending dissection, which can cause aortic rupture and death; chronic stable angina is not the characteristic complication.
explanation_incorrect.E: Dissection is not an infectious process; antibiotics play no role in the acute management.

educationalObjective: Treat Stanford type A dissection (ascending aorta) surgically, and anticipate acute aortic regurgitation and cardiac tamponade as complications.

subject: Cardiovascular
subtopic: Aortic dissection and traumatic aortic rupture
vignette: A 68-year-old man with hypertension and a bicuspid aortic valve presents with sudden-onset, severe chest pain that he describes as tearing, radiating to his interscapular back. His right arm blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg while his left arm blood pressure is 158/92 mm Hg. Chest x-ray shows a widened mediastinum.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: Aortic dissection is a longitudinal intimal tear forming a false lumen, associated with hypertension (the strongest risk factor), bicuspid aortic valve, and inherited connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome. It presents with tearing, sudden-onset chest pain radiating to the back, often with markedly unequal blood pressure in the arms when the tear involves the subclavian origin, and a widened mediastinum on chest x-ray.

explanation_incorrect.A: An acute MI presents with crushing substernal pain, not tearing pain radiating to the back, and would not produce a 62 mm Hg interarm systolic difference or widened mediastinum.
explanation_incorrect.B: Pulmonary embolism causes pleuritic pain, dyspnea, and tachycardia with hypoxia, and does not create unequal arm blood pressures or mediastinal widening.
explanation_incorrect.D: A ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm presents with a pulsatile abdominal mass, abdominal/back pain, and resistant hypotension — not markedly unequal arm pressures.
explanation_incorrect.E: Acute pericarditis causes positional pleuritic chest pain with diffuse ST elevation; it does not cause a widened mediastinum or interarm blood pressure difference.

educationalObjective: Recognize tearing chest pain radiating to the back with unequal arm blood pressures and mediastinal widening as aortic dissection.

subject: Cardiovascular
subtopic: Aortic dissection and traumatic aortic rupture
vignette: A 60-year-old man with poorly controlled blood pressure readings around 180/105 mm Hg presents to the emergency department with sudden, severe chest pain radiating to the back. CT angiography confirms a dissection flap extending from the aortic root into the descending thoracic aorta.
question: Which of the following is the strongest risk factor for this condition?

options.text: Family history of connective tissue disease

explanation_correct: Hypertension is the strongest risk factor for aortic dissection, which is a longitudinal intimal tear forming a false lumen. Other associations include bicuspid aortic valve and inherited connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome. This patient's poorly controlled blood pressure is the key predisposing factor in the vignette.

explanation_incorrect.A: Tobacco smoking is the strongest risk factor for abdominal aortic aneurysm, not for aortic dissection.
explanation_incorrect.C: Bicuspid aortic valve is an associated risk factor for dissection, but it is weaker than hypertension.
explanation_incorrect.D: Male sex is not listed as the strongest risk factor for aortic dissection.
explanation_incorrect.E: A family history of connective tissue disease (eg, Marfan syndrome) is an associated condition, not the strongest risk factor.

educationalObjective: Recall that hypertension is the strongest risk factor for aortic dissection (whereas smoking is strongest for abdominal aortic aneurysm).
